active_paradigms.idea: Conflict-graph-based construction: build a precedence/conflict graph between transactions and use topological-layer decomposition plus simulated annealing on the graph ordering
active_paradigms.description: Instead of blind greedy sampling, precompute pairwise conflict costs between transactions (for each pair i,j, the cost added if j follows i, derivable from shared keys and read/write patterns). Build a weighted directed graph where edge weight i->j is the delay incurred by placing j after i. Then construct an initial schedule via a topological-like ordering that repeatedly picks the transaction minimizing total conflict weight to already-placed transactions (a GRASP-style construction using the cheap pairwise-cost table instead of full get_opt_seq_cost calls). This makes each greedy step O(n) instead of O(n * cost-eval), allowing far more multi-start restarts within the same 100s budget. Follow with the existing local search but now with an incremental cost model: cache the pairwise conflict matrix so local search moves can be evaluated in O(n) via delta computation rather than calling get_opt_seq_cost on the full sequence. Wrap in simulated annealing with a geometric cooling schedule (e.g., start temperature = 5% of initial makespan, alpha=0.95) to escape local optima more systematically than the current ad-hoc stagnation logic.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: makespan via far more search iterations enabled by O(1) incremental cost evaluation
active_paradigms.cautions: The pairwise conflict matrix must be validated against workload.get_opt_seq_cost on a few random sequences to confirm the cost model decomposes additively over adjacent pairs; if makespan depends on more than adjacent pairs (e.g., longest-path through conflict chains), model it as a DAG longest-path computation per candidate ordering instead. Keep the final reported makespan computed with workload.get_opt_seq_cost to guarantee correctness.
active_paradigms.approach_type: custom conflict-graph annealing with cached incremental costs

active_paradigms.idea: Exact lower-bound-guided branch and bound with memoized partial-schedule costs for the smallest workload, and beam search for larger ones
active_paradigms.description: Compute a strong lower bound on makespan: for each key, the transactions accessing it form a chain that must be partially serialized; the maximum over keys of the sum of per-transaction processing along that key's conflict chain gives a lower bound. Use beam search over partial schedules: maintain B (e.g., 50-200) partial orderings, at each depth extend each beam entry with the k most promising next transactions (evaluated with workload.get_opt_seq_cost on the partial prefix plus an admissible completion heuristic = lower bound on remaining cost). Prune beam entries whose partial cost + lower bound already exceeds the best-known full solution. For the smallest workload (if n is small enough, roughly n<=15), run full branch and bound with this bound to reach proven optimality. Allocate the 100s budget proportionally: exact search on small instances, wide beam search on large ones, reusing the current ILS result as the initial upper bound to prune aggressively.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: makespan, especially closing the gap to optimality on small workloads where beam search with good bounds can beat ILS
active_paradigms.cautions: The lower bound must be admissible (never overestimate) or pruning will discard optimal solutions; verify by checking that bound <= cost of any complete schedule. Cache get_opt_seq_cost results for prefixes in a dict keyed by tuple to avoid recomputation. Watch the deadline carefully — beam search cost grows as B*k*n per depth, so tune B to finish within budget with margin.
active_paradigms.approach_type: beam search / branch-and-bound with admissible lower bounds

active_paradigms.idea: Key-centric decomposition: schedule per-key transaction chains first, then merge chains via a sequence-alignment/merge heuristic
active_paradigms.description: Reframe the problem: for each hot key, the set of transactions touching it must appear in some relative order; the makespan is driven by how well these per-key orders interleave. First, for each key, order its transactions by a local criterion (e.g., by total conflict load or by a locally optimized order found via small-scale exhaustive search on just that key's transaction subset). Then treat the problem as merging these per-key chains into one global sequence: use a variant of Huffman-style merging / iterative chain merging where at each step the next transaction chosen is the head of the chain whose keys are most 'ready' (all its key-chains' earlier transactions already placed), breaking ties by evaluating a short lookahead with workload.get_opt_seq_cost. This gives a structurally-informed initial solution that respects conflict chains rather than a random greedy start. Feed this into the existing ILS as the starting point and also run it with randomized tie-breaking as additional restarts. The key insight is that the current algorithm wastes most of its budget on random restarts that ignore the conflict-chain structure entirely.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: makespan via structurally-informed initial solutions that ILS can refine faster than random starts
active_paradigms.cautions: Deadlock risk: per-key chains may be mutually inconsistent (cycle), so implement chain merging as a greedy ready-set simulation (like topological sort with priority) rather than strict chain enforcement; when a transaction's chain predecessors conflict, fall back to conflict-weight ordering. Validate every candidate with workload.get_opt_seq_cost before accepting.
